stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Contemporary accounts of social category learning propose that children build social categories from experience.
Despite the central role of experience in these accounts, we still know relatively little about how children learn social categories from their environment.

Theories in other domains of developmental science have benefited from empirical work characterizing the structure of children's experience; this work suggests that children's environments contain regularities that shape developmental outcomes by structuring the information available for learning.

We propose that a similar approach can advance theories of racial category learning: characterizing the regularities present in children's environments is critical to understand how racial category representations are formed.

Using U.S. children's books as a tractable, developmentally-relevant source of input to children, we employ corpus-analytic methods to examine two input properties known to influence category learning: frequency and contextual structure.

We find that characters from minoritized racial groups are less frequent than their base-rate in the population (Study 1) and that there are systematic differences in the contextual themes associated with different racial groups (Study 2).
Together, these findings suggest that children's books contain distributional regularities along dimensions known to shape category representations.

More broadly, by characterizing the structure of children's experience, this work contributes to a larger effort in developmental science to better understand the environmental regularities from which children learn.

Characterizing the input to racial category learning: Evidence from corpus analyses of children's books It is well documented that children around the world develop preferences and make assumptions about people based on characteristics associated with racial groups 1 , including physical features, culture, religion, and/or language (Farago et al., 2015; Hirschfeld, 1995; Hughes et al., 2023; Levy & Hughes, 2009; Quintana, 1998; Raabe & Beelmann, 2011).

text.text: The development of these preferences and assumptions is believed to start with the learning of racial categories (Averhart & Bigler, 1997; Barrett & Davis, 2008; Bigler & Liben, 2007; Doyle & Aboud, 1995; Katz et al., 1975; McGlothlin & Killen, 2005); therefore, understanding how children learn these categories and how this learning can be modified by experience is a critical part of supporting children's healthy socio-emotional development (Durlak et al., 2011; Marcelo & Yates, 2019; McCall et al., 2022; Skinner-Dorkenoo et al., 2023; Waxman, 2021).

For example, in the United States, children's experiences are likely to include racially segregated neighborhoods and schools, lack of racial diversity among people in leadership positions, and stereotyped media depictions (Hughes & Watford, 2022; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021; Salter et al., 2018).

text.text: Despite this broad agreement that children learn racial categories from their experience with the statistical structure in their environment, a central challenge remains in explaining how children build racial categories from their experience.

text.text: The studies reported here take a corpus-analytic approach to examine a developmentally-relevant source of input: children's books.
As we describe in more detail below, children's books are ubiquitous in the lives of young U.S. children and have also been used in studies attempting to improve racial attitudes in children.
Of course, books are only one of the many sources of information from which children may learn social categories.

But as in previous work sampling children's environments (e.g., Clerkin et al., 2017; Lavi-Rotbain & Arnon, 2023; Montag et al., 2015; Lewis et al., 2022; Sugden et al., 2014), we start with a tractable, developmentally-relevant source of input as a window into the structure of children's experience; in other words, we use the information present in children's books as a measurable source of input to children.
text.formatted: But as in previous work sampling children's environments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Clerkin et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Lavi-Rotbain & Arnon, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Montag et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Lewis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Sugden et al., 2014)</ref>, we start with a tractable, developmentally-relevant source of input as a window into the structure of children's experience; in other words, we use the information present in children's books as a measurable source of input to children.

text.text: To guide our characterization of this input to children, we turn to research on category learning.
This large literature suggests that two properties of experience might be especially important for shaping category representations: frequency and contextual structure.

The frequency or rate with which category members are encountered and the distributional contexts in which category members are encountered influence the familiarity and accessibility of categories, the features associated with those categories, and how they are differentiated from one another (Arnon, 2015; Bullinaria & Levy, 2007; Carvalho et al., 2021; Ellis, 2002; Kruschke, 1996; Landauer & Dumais, 1997; McClelland & Rogers, 2004).
text.formatted: The frequency or rate with which category members are encountered and the distributional contexts in which category members are encountered influence the familiarity and accessibility of categories, the features associated with those categories, and how they are differentiated from one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Arnon, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Bullinaria & Levy, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Carvalho et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Ellis, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Kruschke, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Landauer & Dumais, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">McClelland & Rogers, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, if real-world input does contribute to learning racial categories, then we would expect to see systematic differences with regards to both the frequency and the contexts surrounding the depiction of different racial groups.
Studies 1 and 2 were designed to test these predictions by assessing whether these regularities are systematically present in children's books.
In what follows, we first present a brief review of the literature documenting the learning of racial categories early in development.

Next, we review the literature on category learning and representational change across the lifespan, noting how the literature on the input features that influence category learning has made limited contact with the literature on the early learning of racial categories.
Studies 1 and 2 then follow.

In the General Discussion, we consider the implications of these findings for theories of racial category learning, discuss how characterizing children's input may inform efforts to modify developmental trajectories, and identify important directions for future research.

It is well-documented that during infancy and early childhood children begin to attend to and differentiate people based on characteristics associated with multiple socially-relevant dimensions -including those typically associated with racial groups (e.g., skin color, facial features, hair texture, language, and/or religious markers; for reviews, see Aboud & Skeerry, 1984; Katz, 2003; Quintana, 1998; Raabe & Beelmann, 2011; Waxman, 2021).

text.text: In other words, before their first birthday, White infants have formed a distinction between White faces and faces of people from minoritized racial groups, while failing to differentiate faces within those minoritized racial groups 2 .

text.text: Together, this evidence suggests that the early learning of racial categories is experience-dependent.

Children growing up in social contexts like the U.S. are likely to experience a lack of racial diversity among people in positions of authority such as teachers and doctors, be exposed to media that promotes racial stereotypes, or live in neighborhoods or attend schools that are racially homogeneous (Hughes et al., 2023; Hughes & Watford, 2022; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021; Salter et al., 2018).

text.text: Yet, despite the central role of experience in these accounts, we still know little about how children learn racial categories from the regularities in their environment.
Work across developmental science shows that characterizing the regularities in children's environments is a critical step towards building better developmental theories.

For example, theories of language learning have a long history of integrating insights from empirical work documenting the statistics in child-directed language to refine theory and to identify targets for intervention (Anderson et al., 2021; Hart & Risley, 1995; Hoff, 2003; Suskind, 2016; Rowe, 2012 : Rowe & Snow, 2020).

text.text: We propose that this approach is equally beneficial for theories of social category learning: characterizing the regularities present in children's environments is a critical part of understanding how racial category representations are formed and how to modify them.

Based on well-established findings on input features that influence category learning, we hypothesize that there will be systematic differences in children's experiences with racial groups in both their frequency and distributional contexts; we review this literature in the next section.

From birth and throughout the lifespan, humans are remarkable at encoding the statistical structure of their environment, and this ability supports a wide range of cognitive and social processes (Fiser & Lengyel, 2022; Isbilen & Christiansen, 2022; Romberg & Saffran, 2010; Ruba et al., 2022; Shapiro & Turk-Browne, 2015).

text.text: In particular, a large literature converges on frequency and distributional contexts as two critical features of the input that influence the familiarity and accessibility of categories, the features associated with those categories, and how they are differentiated.

Across domains, learners are sensitive to how often entities occur (Arnon, 2015; Carvalho et al., 2021; Ellis, 2002; Kruschke, 1996; Lavi-Rotbain & Arnon, 2021; 2022; 2023; Yang & Worthy, 2025) and the contexts in which they occur (Bullinaria & Levy, 2007; Gómez, 2002; Günther et al., 2019; Hamilton & Gifford, 1976; Jones et al., 2017; Jones & Mewhort, 2007; Landauer & Dumais, 1997; Reeder et al., 2013; Rhodes et al., 2012; Richie & Bhatia, 2021; McClelland & Rogers, 2004; Vlach & Sandhofer, 2011), using frequency and distributional contexts to form expectations about category structure and category membership.

text.text: Through these processes, environmental regularities shape how categories are represented, the features learners associate with categories, and how categories are differentiated from one another.
Sensitivity to statistical structure, however, can also produce inaccurate representations when environmental regularities are misleading.

For example, children develop misconceptions about scientific concepts such as the shape of the Earth and produce overregularization errors such as "mouses" and "goed" (Berko, 1958; Carey, 1985; Elman, 2001; Hanley et al., 2016; Vosniadou & Brewer, 1992; Waller et al., 2024).

For instance, everyday experience provides little evidence that the Earth is a sphere orbiting the sun, leading children to infer that the Earth is flat (Vosniadou & Brewer, 1992).

text.text: We propose that learning racial categories is another domain in which the statistical structure to which children are exposed may give rise to inaccurate representations.

Systematic differences in the frequency and distributional contexts associated with different racial groups would lead children to represent racial groups as increasingly dissimilar, thereby contributing to the development of racial bias (Averhart & Bigler, 1997; Barrett & Davis, 2008; Bigler & Liben, 2007; Doyle & Aboud, 1995; Katz et al., 1975; McGlothlin & Killen, 2005).

text.text: If so, then we would expect children to encounter White individuals more frequently than individuals from minoritized racial groups (Study 1) and to systematically encounter different racial groups embedded in different distributional contexts (Study 2).
As a proxy for children's experience, we focus on children's picture books.

We focus on children's books because they are ubiquitous in the lives of young U.S. children -many families read to their children daily since birth (Patel et al., 2024; Young et al., 1998) and educators often use picture books in preschool and kindergarten classrooms (Kemple et al., 2016).

text.text: If children's input does contribute to learning racial categories, then we would expect to see that characters from minoritized racial backgrounds should be underrepresented relative to White characters in children's books.
To evaluate this question, it is important to define what is meant by 'underrepresented'.
One might argue that, because of the demographics of the United States, it would be expected that most characters in children's books available in the U.S. would be White.
According to 2022 estimates, 58.9% of the total U.S. population identifies as White non-Hispanic (US Census); we will evaluate our findings relative to these estimates.

Existing work suggests that characters from minoritized racial groups are less common in children's books relative to characters from the majority group (Bramlett-Solomon & Roeder, 2008; Chung, 2019;  Cooperative Children's Book Center, n.d.; Koss, 2015; Koss & Paciga, 2020; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021).

For example, some studies report that 25% or less of the book corpus analyzed depicts characters from minoritized racial groups (e.g., Hughes-Hassell et al., 2009; Iwamoto, 1996; Lee, 2017), whereas this figure approaches or surpasses 50% in other studies (e.g., Edmonds, 1986; Hughes-Hassell & Cox, 2010; McDaniel, 2020).

text.text: Because existing studies differ in which racial groups were reported, we adopted a coding scheme that contrasted minoritized characters with White characters.
Although this approach necessarily obscures important differences among minoritized groups, it is methodologically necessary so that consistent estimates can be extracted across corpora.
We conducted a literature search following the PRISMA approach (Liberati et al., 2009) (see Figure 1).

text.text: We searched Google Scholar and Scopus between March and June 2022 using the following terms: ("character" OR "protagonist") AND ("child" OR "children") AND ("book" OR "picture book" OR "literature") AND ("race" OR "ethnicity") AND ("diversity" OR "representation").

This search retrieved 826,000 results in Google Scholar and 4 results in Scopus, making exhaustive screening infeasible; therefore, we screened the abstracts of the first 500 Google Scholar results and all 4 Scopus results (N = 504).
Additional sources (N = 17) were identified through related-publication searches, reference lists, and our own data (reported in the Supplemental Materials, S1).
As shown in Figure 1, abstract screening of these 521 sources, using the inclusion criteria described below, identified 40 potentially eligible sources for full-text review.

text.text: Fulltext screening resulted in a final sample of 20 sources that satisfied all inclusion criteria and were included in the data extraction step (these are indicated by an asterisk (*) in the Reference section).

Sources were eligible if they: (1) were peer-reviewed journal papers, theses, or proceedings (book sources were excluded because they are not primary sources); (2) analyzed children's books that were available to children in the United States (we did not include analyses of textbooks, television programs, or materials intended for adolescents or adults); (3) coded the race of human characters -including White characters and at least one other racial group -and reported sufficient information to determine character countsfoot_1 ; (4) were written in English.

text.text: First, for each paper, we extracted the authors, title, and year of publication.
This information was used to create a shortened citation (e.g., "Crisp et al., 2016") to be used in figures.

Next, to calculate effect sizes, for each study we extracted the number of human characters that belonged to minoritized racial groups, the number of human characters that belonged to the majority racial group, and the total number of human characters.
These data were extracted from the text, table, figures, or a combination of these, typically found in the Results section or the supplemental materials.

Due to different studies employing different coding schemes (e.g., coded the presence of animal and/or inanimate characters; included an "indeterminate" or "unknown" category), we first extracted the number of characters belonging to either the dominant racial group (i.e., indicated in the paper as White, European, or Caucasian) or to a minoritized racial group (i.e., characters coded as Asian, Biracial or Multiracial, Black or African American, Latine, Middle Eastern or Arab, Native American, Person of color, or Racial/Ethnic minority).
The sum of the count of the two categories was entered as the total number of human characters.

Using this sum as the denominator when calculating the proportions of characters from minoritized racial groups and the dominant racial group ensured that the proportions were comparable across all studies included.

Note that in some cases (e.g., when additional categories such as animal or inanimate character were coded or when multiple characters per book were coded) this might result in the percentages reported in the meta-analysis differing from those reported in the source and/or the total number of characters in our analysis differing from the total number of books reported in the paper.

For each paper we additionally coded the following variables: (i) which characters were coded (only one protagonist, main characters, all characters); (ii) the publication year or range of publication years of the books coded in that source; (iii) how many books were coded; and (iv) how the books were selected for inclusion (award-winning and/or best-selling status; time period; school libraries).
These variables are reported in the Supplemental Materials (S2).

Finally, to address the possibility that there could be overlap in book titles across the papers included in the meta-analysis -which could create unknown interdependencies in the datawe additionally coded the degree of overlap in book titles across the sources for which this information was available; this variable was used to conduct the sensitivity analysis reported in the Supplemental Materials (S2).
A random effect meta-analysis was performed to estimate the pooled frequency of characters from minoritized racial groups.
Confidence intervals for individual studies were calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method and the between-study variance was estimated using the DerSimonian-Laird technique.
Data were pooled using the inverse-variance method and the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation was used to calculate an overall proportion.
A value of 0.411 was used to specify the null hypothesis (i.e., that there is no underrepresentation of characters from minoritized racial groups relative to U.S. demographics).
This number was obtained by calculating the complement of the proportion of the U.S. population who identifies as White non-Hispanic (58.9%; U.S. Census Bureau) (i.e., 1 -0.589 = 0.411).
Between-study heterogeneity was assessed visually using a forest plot and quantified using the I² statistic; heterogeneity was considered to be high if I² was greater than 75% (Higgins et al, 2003).

Finally, to address the possibility that different sources could include many of the same book titles, we recalculated the meta-analytical frequency estimate including only sources for which we are certain there is no or low crosssource overlap; those analyses, reported in detail in the Supplemental Materials (S2), showed that the degree of overlap was very small and unlikely to influence the meta-analytical frequency estimate.
Taken together, the results of this meta-analysis suggest that characters from minoritized racial groups are underrepresented in children's books relative to their base-rate in the U.S. population.

As of 2022, an estimated 41% of the U.S. population belongs to minoritized racial groups, but our aggregate estimate suggests that only 25% of characters in children's books are people from minoritized racial groups.

By synthesizing evidence across existing corpus studies, this meta-analysis provides the first aggregate estimate of the frequency with which racial groups are depicted in children's books, allowing a more precise test of frequency differences.
In Study 2 we tested the hypothesis that there are systematic differences in the distributional contexts surrounding the depiction of racial groups in children's books.

Existing evidence suggests that children may encounter systematically different information about characters from different racial groups through the narratives in which those characters are embedded.

For example, a content analysis of 218 books marketed to infants and toddlers showed that when characters from minoritized racial groups were depicted, the books still centered White characters (Hughes-Hassell & Cox, 2010).

text.text: Here we expand this existing work in two important ways.
First, we use a larger corpus of books and include a wider range of publication years relative to prior work -both important for the generalizability of the findings.

Second, we use a measure of mutual information to quantify associations between racial groups and thematic contexts while accounting for differences in the base rates of both thematic contexts and racial groups within the corpus.
This allows us to identify whether particular thematic contexts are disproportionately associated with specific racial groups beyond what would be expected from their overall frequencies alone.

As we describe below, we analyzed a comprehensive collection of children's books featuring characters from minoritized racial backgrounds in which each book has been categorized according to its central narrative theme (Aronson et al., 2018).

text.text: We treated these themes as an operationalization of context -under the assumption that characters appearing in books with the same theme are embedded in more similar contexts than characters appearing in books with different themes.
If different racial groups are systematically associated with different distributional contexts, thematic context and racial group should be statistically non-independent.
>Method

text.text: We searched the Diverse BookFinder corpus (diversebookfinder.org) to document the number of books depicting characters from minoritized racial backgrounds in each thematic context.
Because the collection systematically catalogs books according to both racial group and thematic context, it provides a unique resource for examining the association between these variables.
The collection in the Diverse BookFinder includes all literature for children and youth featuring characters from minoritized backgrounds published in the US since 2002.

We restricted the corpus to "Picture books" (using the "Form" filter) and used the "Central Theme Categories" filter to obtain the count of books depicting characters of each racial group in each theme.

We also restricted the analysis to six racial groups and five themes that showed the most variability across racial groups in prior work (Aronson et al., 2018; Laboy et al., 2023) foot_2 ; we excluded categories that were either infrequently represented or showed little variation across groups because such categories contribute limited information about associations between racial group and thematic context.

text.text: The five themes -i.e., contexts -included in our analysis are: Any child, Centering Culture and Identity, Cross-group, Folklore, and Oppression.

Books in the Any Child category feature narratives about everyday topics and adventures in which the racial group of the character is not central to the narrative (e.g., 'Jabari Jumps' by Gaia Cornwall).
By contrast, books in the Centering Culture and Identity category feature characters in which racial identity is central to the narrative (e.g., 'Bilal Cooks Daal' by Aisha Saeed).
Books in the Cross Group category depict interactions between racial groups (e.g., 'A New Kind of Wild' by Zara Gonzalez Hoang).
Books in the Folklore category feature aspects of tradition, cultural rituals, or values of a group of people (e.g., 'The Orphan and the Polar Bear' by Sakiasi Qaunaq).
Finally, books in the Oppression category depict groupbased injustice and struggles for justice (e.g., 'Separate is Never Equal' by Duncan Tonatiuh).
We treated these thematic categories as a proxy for the semantic contexts in which characters are depicted.
Under this operationalization, books assigned to the same thematic category are assumed to provide more similar contextual information than books assigned to different categories.

Although prior work already suggests that young children are sensitive to thematic differences in narratives (Aronson et al., 2016; Cameron et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2025; Gasser et al., 2022), future research will be needed to determine how children learn from the thematic categories examined here.

text.text: The six racial groups included in the analysis are: Asian/Pacific Islander/Asian American; Biracial/Multiracial/Mixed Race; Black/African/African American; First/Native Nations/American Indian/Indigenous; Latine/Hispanic/Latin American; Middle Eastern/North African/Arab.
For ease of reading, these groups will be shortened in the text and in figures as follows: "Asian", "Multiracial", "Black", "Native Peoples", "Latine", "Middle Eastern".
As typical of naturally-occurring data, the levels of the two variables analyzed here show unequal base rates.

For example, some racial groups are represented more frequently than others (e.g., Black characters are more common than Latine characters), and some thematic contexts are more common than others (e.g., Centering Culture and Identity books are more common than Oppression books); this makes raw counts difficult to interpret.

Therefore, to analyze the patterns of conditional dependencies in the book collection, we applied a measure of mutual information (Pointwise Mutual Information, PMI; Fano, 1961) to the contingency table of racial groups and themes using the pmi function from the svs package (Plevoets, 2015) in R (R Core Team, 2022).

text.text: PMI corrects for the unequal base rates by quantifying the extent to which a specific group-theme pairing occurs more or less frequently than would be expected from the overall frequencies of the group and theme alone.

Conceptually, PMI compares the observed frequency of a specific racial group-theme pairing (e.g., Black-Oppression) to the frequency that would be expected if racial group and theme were statistically independent.

A PMI score of 0 indicates independence; positive values indicate that a pairing occurs more frequently than expected under an assumption of independence and negative values indicate that it occurs less frequently than expected under an assumption of independence.

To facilitate interpretation, we focus on pairings with PMI scores in the highest and lowest quartiles of the distribution (see red and dark blue cells in Figure 3); these pairings are the strongest positive and negative departures from statistical independence and therefore provide the clearest evidence of systematic associations between racial groups and thematic contexts.

text.text: Overall, different racial groups appear to be more strongly associated with certain themes.

Specifically, Black characters dominate the Oppression theme (PMI=0.64), Native People (PMI=0.75) and Latine (PMI=0.47) characters are strongly associated with the Centering Culture and Identity theme, and Middle Eastern (PMI=1.55) and Asian characters (PMI=0.92) are likely to be portrayed in the Folklore theme.

Finally, there are also strong associations between Multiracial characters and the Any Child theme (PMI= 0.98), as well as between Black (PMI=0.29) and Middle Eastern/Arab (PMI=0.26) characters and the Cross Group theme -though the last two were weaker relative to the other themes positively associated with each group.
The lowest scores -by hypothesis, the pairings that are least likely to be experienced by U.S. children -offer us further insight into the distributional contexts.

Middle Eastern (PMI=-1.95) and Native Peoples (PMI=-0.80) were unlikely to be portrayed in books with the Any Child theme (recall that these racial groups were also most frequently depicted in the Folklore and the Centering Culture and Identity themes, respectively).
Latine (PMI=-0.96), Multiracial (PMI=-0.95), and Asian (PMI=-0.90) characters were unlikely to be depicted in books about Oppression.
Finally, Multiracial (PMI=-1.78), Native People (PMI=-1.26), and Black (PMI=-1.1) characters were unlikely to be portrayed in books with Folklore messages.

Study 2 suggests that, even when the relative frequencies of each group and contextual theme are considered, there are systematic differences pertaining to how often certain racial groups and thematic contexts are likely to occur -or not occur -together.
First, Black characters were disproportionately associated with books about Oppression, while Asian, Latine, and Multiracial characters were underrepresented in this thematic context.

Second, Middle Eastern/Arab and Native Peoples were disproportionally depicted in Folklore or Centering Culture and Identity books, with these same groups being unlikely to be depicted in Any Child books.
Third, Latine and Asian characters were disproportionally depicted in Folklore or Centering Culture and Identity books.

While it is important for children to learn about cultural histories and practices (White & Wanless, 2019), the systematic co-occurrence of particular racial groups and thematic contexts may provide children with distributional evidence that certain groups belong with certain kinds of narratives.

text.text: To the extent that children are sensitive to these distributional regularities, such patterns may contribute to the learning and differentiation of racial categories.
The studies reported here aimed to characterize the structure of experience from which children may learn racial categories.

Drawing on theories of category learning, we focused on two properties of experience that are known to influence category formation and representational structure across domains: frequency and contextual structure.

Consistent with our predictions, Study 1 showed systematic differences in the frequency with which racial groups are depicted in children's books, such that characters from minoritized racial groups were underrepresented relative to their prevalence in the U.S. population.
Study 2 showed systematic differences in distributional contexts, such that different racial groups were systematically associated with different thematic contexts.
Together, these findings suggest that children's books contain regularities that could plausibly support the learning of racial categories.

In what follows, we discuss the implications of these findings for theories of racial category learning, consider how characterizing children's input may inform efforts to modify developmental trajectories, and outline directions for future research.
The ability to learn from the statistical distribution of data is one of the most well-established findings in developmental science.

From birth, infants are remarkably adept at learning the distribution of events in their environment, and this ability is thought to underlie infants and children's ability to segment words from speech, acquire visual categories, establish word-to-object mappings, and learn to recognize emotions (Fiser & Lengyel, 2022; Isbilen & Christiansen, 2022; Romberg & Saffran, 2010; Ruba et al., 2022; Shapiro & Turk-Browne, 2015).

text.text: By examining children's books as one measurable source of developmentally-relevant input, the present studies provide evidence that children's experience includes regularities both in the frequency with which racial groups are encountered and in the contexts in which they are encountered.

Research on category learning shows that category representations are shaped by the frequency with which exemplars are encountered and by the distributional contexts in which they appear (Arnon, 2015; Bullinaria & Levy, 2007; Carvalho et al., 2021; Ellis, 2002; Kruschke, 1996; Landauer & Dumais, 1997; McClelland & Rogers, 2004).

text.text: The present findings suggest that both sources of information vary systematically across racial groups in children's books.

From a statistical learning perspective, these regularities constitute potential learning signals: repeated exposure to these patterns may provide information about which racial groups are common and about which narratives and experiences tend to co-occur with which groups; in turn, this input may provide distributional information that differentiates racial groups from one another in children's mental representations.
In other words, if children encode these regularities, they may gradually accumulate different expectations about different racial groups.
In this way, frequency and contextual structure may be dimensions of experience through which everyday experiences contribute to the formation and differentiation of racial category representations.

More broadly, we believe that characterizing the statistical structure of children's experiences, guided by what is known from the categorization and representational change literatures, should become a central component of research on racial category learning, much as analyses of child-directed language have become central to theories of language development (Anderson et al., 2021; Hart & Risley, 1995; Hoff, 2003; Suskind, 2016; Rowe, 2012 : Rowe & Snow, 2020).

text.text: An implication of this perspective is that explaining the development of racial categories requires understanding not only the representations children possess, but also the statistical regularities from which those representations are learned.

By identifying systematic differences in both the frequency and contextual structure of racial representations in children's books, the present studies provide a step toward specifying the environmental inputs that may give rise to children's emerging beliefs, expectations, and attitudes about racial groups.

A shift toward studying the structure of children's experiences, guided by insights from the categorization and representational change literatures, has the potential to advance a more mechanistic understanding of how ow everyday environments contribute to the emergence of racial categories -and, potentially, racial biases -in early childhood.

Importantly, understanding the structure of children's experience also has the potential to allow us to change the learning trajectory of racial categorization, and thus interrupt the development of racial biases.

If children's representations of racial groups are shaped by the statistical regularities they encounter, then characterizing those regularities may help identify features of experience that can be targeted for intervention -a critical goal towards improving all children's well-being and reducing inequalities (Marcelo & Yates, 2019; Skinner-Dorkenoo et al., 2023; Waxman, 2021).

text.text: The present studies were not designed to test interventions.

At the same time, if frequency and contextual structure are important components of the input from which children learn racial categories, then these same features of experience may be promising targets for future intervention efforts.

Therefore, one implication is that interventions may be most effective when they modify the same dimensions of experience that contribute to category learning: if frequency and contextual structure play a role in shaping racial category representations, then interventions that alter these properties of children's experience may promote greater perceived similarity across groups.

Based on the results reported here, one hypothesis is that children's representations of racial groups should become more similar if different racial groups are encountered with more comparable frequencies and if thematic contexts are distributed more evenly across groups.

Importantly, these two factors likely to not operate independently; for example, in the context of book exposure, merely increasing the frequency of exposure to racially diverse characters might not be sufficient to increase intergroup similarity in the absence of more uniform distributions of thematic contexts.
The contribution of each factorand their interaction -will be critical to determine in future empirical work.

It also remains an open question whether exposure to a more uniform distribution (both of frequency and of contexts) would be sufficient to alter category representations shaped by prior experience, or whether one would need to oversample from the other end of the distribution -that is, to increase exposure to groups and to group-theme pairings in the inverse of the frequency documented in the present studies.
Distinguishing among these possibilities will require experimental and longitudinal work tracking changes in children's representations.
The evidence reported here leaves several important questions for future work.
First, it will be important for future work to determine if the statistics observed in children's books generalize to other aspects of children's experiences and to other social groups.

The present studies focused on books because they provide a tractable, developmentally relevant source of input and because existing work suggests that the structure of experience observed here is likely not restricted to books or even to media (Bramlett-Solomon & Roeder, 2008; Hughes & Watford, 2022; Roberts & Rizzo, 2021; Salter et al., 2018; Tukachinsky et al., 2015; Vargas & Verstynen, 2025).

text.text: Second, it will be important to document whether these patterns remain stable or change over time - Third, it will be important to directly relate individual variation in experience -whether naturally occurring or experimentally manipulated -to changes in children's representations of racial categories.
These will be critical to develop better theoretical models of experience-dependent development of racial categories, as well as to develop better intervention tools.

We would be remiss to not mention the importance of using valid and reliable measures to assess changes in racial categories and social preferences; existing media-based intervention studies have often relied on measures with unknown psychometric properties (Aboud et al., 2012), limiting the conclusions that can be drawn about developmental change.

Black characters were also the most common group in the corpus examined in Study 2; does exposure to one (or a few) minoritized racial groups lead to generalization of attitudes to other minoritized racial groups?

We compiled the year of publication, author name, and illustrator name for each of these 100 titles, and coded them according to the categories described below.

text.text: What is the distribution of the main characters' race in contemporary popular U.S. picture books?
To identify the main character of each book, the coders took into consideration the title, illustrations, synopsis of the book, and the book pages.
If the main character of a book -the character that is present in most pages and is the target of the plot -was considered human, their race was coded as 'dominant' (i.e., White) or 'minoritized'.
If the main character of a book was considered to not be human, then it was coded as either 'nonhuman animal' (thereafter, 'animal') or 'object'.
If no main character could be identified, the coders used 'undetermined' (1% of the corpus).
The coders reached 91% agreement on this category.

To examine the distribution of main characters in the corpus, we compared in an omnibus analysis the number of books in each of the main character categories ('dominant racial group', 'minoritized racial group', 'animal', and 'object'); this allows us to document if the categories were equally distributed in the corpus.

We followed up on this omnibus analysis by sequentially comparing the categories based on their frequency (i.e., sequential pairwise comparisons from the most to least frequent character category); this analysis also included a planned test of the hypothesis that White characters would be more frequent than characters from minoritized racial groups -which we tested by directly comparing the frequency of these two categories.
Because of the multiple pairwise comparisons conducted in this analysis, we adjusted the p-values using the Bonferroni method.

text.text: As can be seen, the categories are not evenly distributed in the corpus.

Specifically, more than half of the books in the corpus (66%) depict nonhuman characters, with 56% of the books including an animal as the main character and 10% of the books in the corpus including an object as the main character.
With regards to human characters, 31% of the characters in the corpus were members of the dominant racial group, while 2% of the characters in the corpus were members of a minoritized racial group.
An omnibus chi-square test confirmed that these four categories are not equally distributed, !
A sequential comparison of the character categories in this corpus showed that animals were more frequently depicted as main characters than White characters (!
2 (1) = 7.2, p = 0.03) and that White characters were more frequent than objects as main characters (!
2 (1) = 10.8, p = 0.0004); there was no statistically significance evidence that the frequency of object main characters and characters belonging to minoritized racial groups differed (!
2 (1) = 5.3, p = 0.08) (all p-values corrected using the Bonferroni method).

Finally, to examine the hypothesis that children's popular picture books are more likely to depict White characters than characters belonging to minoritized racial groups, we directly compared these two categories.

A chi-square test showed that in this corpus of popular picture books, the number of books depicting White characters is significantly larger than the number of books depicting characters belonging to minoritized racial groups, !

text.text: The analysis reported in the previous section showed that animal main characters were the most common category in the corpus of popular books analyzed.

Many forms of media for children include nonhuman characters (such as animals or objects) depicted performing actions typically associated with humans (e.g., wearing clothes, driving a vehicle, having friendships; Casey et al., 2021; Goldstein & Alperson, 2020; McCabe et al., 2011).

text.text: While fantasy and make-believe are ubiquitous components childhood in Western societies (Hofferth & Sandberg, 2001), if children's picture books are more likely to depict nonhuman characters performing human actions than human characters belonging to minoritized racial groups, this may have consequences for children's emerging understanding of race-based hierarchies.

text.text: For White children, such statistics may increase children's tendency to anthropomorphize animals and hinder recognition of the shared humanity among people from all racial and ethnic backgrounds.

For children belonging to minoritized racial groups, not seeing characters like themselves may result not only in the internalization of racial hierarchies but may also result in limited opportunities for the development of positive self-identity (Koss, 2015; Pérez Huber, Camargo Gonzalez & Solórzano; 2020; Pérez Huber & Solorzano, 2015).

text.text: To examine whether such trends were present in this corpus of popular children's picture books, the presence of human behaviors was coded for the main characters in the corpus.
To code this category, the coders took into consideration the title, illustrations, synopsis of the book, and the book pages.

The main characters were coded as whether they frequently displayed human behaviors (e.g., wearing human clothes, living in a house, driving a vehicle, using human language, having friendships), nonhuman animal behaviors (e.g., laying eggs, eating grass, living in a burrow), or both (when both types of behaviors were present; e.g., talking and laying eggs).

Books in which characters displayed other kinds of behaviors or for which the coders were unable to code this category with certainty from the information available were coded as 'other' (1% of the corpus).
The coders reached 70% agreement on this category.

text.text: As such, we also documented the race of the author and illustrator of the books in this corpus to examine if similar trends were present.
The author and the illustrator of each book were coded as either belonging to the 'dominant' (i.e., White) or 'minoritized' racial group.

The coders followed the coding scheme suggested by the Cooperative Children's Book Center (n.d.), including looking at the author or illustrator's biographies, websites, interviews, association memberships (e.g., Asian/Pacific American Library Association), and family background.
The two coders reached 99% agreement on this category.
The overwhelmingly majority of the creators (authors and illustrators) of the books in the corpus was White (98%), with only 2% of all creators being a member of a minoritized racial group, !
Such a small number of creators belonging to minoritized racial groups precluded any further analysis of trends.
Taken together, these results suggest that these popular contemporary picture books overrepresent White characters.

The results further suggest that animal main characters are not only the most frequent category, but also that these animal characters are likely to be depicted performing behaviors typically associated with humans (e.g., a pigeon driving a bus or a dinosaur having a bedtime routine).

Future work can more directly examine what such regular experience with books depicting anthropomorphized animal characters (but not with characters belonging to minoritized racial groups) may be teaching young children about the social and racial hierarchies entrenched in the United States.
The meta-analysis of proportions reported in Study 1 found evidence of between-study heterogeneity.
Such variation is typically examined by performing a quantitative moderator analysis.
However, the accepted practice is that a quantitative analysis of moderators should include at least 10 studies per moderator (Littell et al., 2008), which is not feasible in this meta-analysis.

text.text: Therefore, due to the small number of sources available in this meta-analysis, we examined the heterogeneity in effect sizes in two ways: through a qualitative description of the sources whose confidence intervals were furthest away from the confidence interval of the pooled point estimate and through a leave-one-out analysis.
We note that, as with any analysis of moderators, these trends are descriptive and cannot be taken as causal evidence (Cuijpers, 2016; Littell et al., 2008).

Third, to address the possibility that different sources could include many of the same book titleswhich would create unknown interdependencies in the data -we conducted a sensitivity analysis after coding the degree of overlap across sources for which the book titles included in the source were available 1 (N=16).

To quantify pairwise overlap, we used the Jaccard Similarity Index, the ratio between the shared items (i.e., the book titles that are common across two sources) and the total unique items (i.e., the unique book titles across the two sources) for each pair of sources.
The average degree of pairwise overlap was 0.06 (SD=0.16, min=0, max=0.98), suggesting an overall very low degree of title overlap across sources.

Most source pairs (84% of all pairs) had a similarity score lower than 0.1; from the remainder sources, 13% of all pairs had a similarity score between 0.1 and 0.39, and 3% had a pairwise similarity score larger than 0.4 (these three sources with the highest overlap were : Koss, 2016; Koss et al., 2017; Moffet, 2016).

We would like to note two features of the dataset that are important for contextualizing the results.
First, these three categories combined (i.e., Christian, Jewish, Muslim) account for a small proportion of the total number of books in this analysis (12%).

Second, the books in the DiverseBook Finder collection are selected for inclusion based on featuring characters from minoritized racial/ethnic groups and then additionally tagged if aspects of religious groups are includedand therefore, these likely do not accurately represent all children's books depicting religious groups.
Because of these two features of the dataset, the results reported here should be viewed as in need of future corroboration.

Specifically, Muslim characters were likely to be depicted in books about cultural practices (PMI=0.39) as well as in cross-group books (PMI=0.37), while unlikely to be depicted in books about Oppression (PMI=-0.82).
Jewish characters were also likely to be depicted in cross-group books (PMI=0.97), while unlikely to be depicted in Any Child books (PMI=-2.47).
Finally, Christian characters were likely to be depicted in Oppression books (PMI=1.33), while unlikely to be depicted in Any Child (PMI=-1.79) or Folklore (PMI=-0.86) books.

As discussed above, we note that these three groups combined are a small proportion of all analyzed books and that, due to the selection process, the titles analyzed might not accurately represent all children's books depicting religious groups; therefore the scores should be regarded with caution.
Nevertheless, these data point at the possibility that there are also systematic differences in the themes that are more -or less -likely to be associated with religious groups.
Because children develop beliefs based on markers of religion or religious practices, it seems likely that the statistics present in books to US children play a part in shaping these beliefs.

Despite efforts to diversify the experiences depicted in children's media, data from recent years does not suggest large increases in the frequency with which characters from minoritized racial groups are depicted in children's literature; for example, the Children's Cooperative Book Center (n.d.) reports modest increases in the number of newly-published books that depict characters from minoritized racial backgrounds, with estimates for recent years not considerably above those reported in Study 1.
Understanding how the structure of children's experiences changes over time will therefore be important for understanding changes in children's opportunities for learning about racial categories.
